# Agent instructions for this repository

This repository is the home of a container image that runs
[OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) for TypeScript development. GitHub Actions
builds and publishes the image to GHCR on every push to `main`, on a schedule,
and on demand. Read [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md) for the layout
and the pipeline, and [docs/updating.md](docs/updating.md) for versioning.

## Environment limits

- Docker and Podman are not available in the default working environment.
  The image is built only by the GitHub Actions workflow, so validate changes
  statically and let CI build them.
- Run the static checks below after touching the corresponding file types;
  they must pass before committing.

| File types                         | Check                                                                       |
| ---------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `*.sh`                             | `shellcheck` and `shfmt -i 2 -d` (must print no diff)                       |
| `*.md`                             | `prettier --check --prose-wrap preserve --embedded-language-formatting off` |
| `*.yml`, `*.yaml` (workflows, k8s) | `yq -e . file`                                                              |
| `*.jsonc`                          | strip `//` comment lines, then parse as JSON (node or jq)                   |

Format changed Markdown with
`prettier --write --prose-wrap preserve --embedded-language-formatting off`
before committing; it pads tables so they stay aligned in a terminal.

## Rules

- **Versions are never hardcoded** in the `Containerfile` or the workflow.
  `scripts/resolve-versions.sh` resolves the current OpenCode and Node LTS at
  CI time; `versions.json` is the pinned record and is updated only by the
  `update-pins` bot PR.
- **Secrets are host-side only.** Never commit a `.env` file, never print or
  echo tokens. `.env.example` is the template; it is baked into the image at
  `/home/opencode/.env.example` for the `env-setup` agent skill.
- **Documentation:** English, in `docs/` as short single-topic pages; link
  every page from the README index and cross-link related pages. Keep
  `README.md` at 100 lines or fewer. Update the affected docs in the same
  change as behavior, configuration, or setup.
- **Commits:** English, Conventional Commits (`feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`,
  `chore:`, ...). Commit after each logical change, not one giant commit.
- **Two AGENTS.md files are different things.** The root file is for agents
  working on this repository. `config/opencode/AGENTS.md` is baked into the
  image and instructs the agent that runs inside it, for TypeScript work.
  Do not mix their concerns.

## After pushing

The push to `main` triggers the `Build` workflow. Watch the run (GitHub
Actions or `gh run list` / `gh run watch`), and on failure read the logs
(`gh run view <id> --log`) before changing anything. The smoke test checks
that the published image starts the server and answers `GET /api/info` with
Basic auth.

# Instructions

## Language rules

- **Conversation with the user:** in the language the user writes in.
- **Code:** identifiers, variables, functions, classes, file names — in English.
- **Code comments:** in English.
- **Git commit messages:** in English, Conventional Commits format (feat:, fix:, docs:, etc.).
- **Documentation, log messages, error messages, CLI output:** in English.

## Style

- Keep code idiomatic and clean.
- Keep changes consistent with the structure, naming and patterns of the
  surrounding code.

## Tooling

The image ships a development toolchain. Prefer these tools over ad-hoc
alternatives.

- Search: `rg` (ripgrep), `fd`, `ast-grep` (also available as `sg`) for
  structural search and rewriting.
- JSON/YAML: `jq`, `yq`.
- Node.js: managed by `mise`. The Node LTS installed at image build time is
  the default. `.nvmrc`, `.node-version`, `.tool-versions` and `mise.toml`
  are honored automatically, and missing versions are installed on demand.
- Python: `python3` with `uv` for scripts (`uv venv`, `uv pip install`,
  `uvx`). Do not install packages into the system interpreter with `pip`.
- Package managers: `npm`, `pnpm` and `yarn` (Corepack reads `packageManager`
  from `package.json`).
- TypeScript: `tsc`, the TypeScript language server and `prettier` are
  installed globally for Node; format changed Markdown with
  `prettier --write --prose-wrap preserve --embedded-language-formatting off`.
- Forge: `gh` for GitHub, `glab` for GitLab (issues, MRs, pipelines,
  releases); Forgejo through the REST API.
- Shell scripts: `shellcheck`, `shfmt`.
- Native builds: `gcc`/`g++`, `make`, Linux headers and the Node headers
  needed by `node-gyp` are available.

## Git and forges

- Commits use `GIT_AUTHOR_*` and `GIT_COMMITTER_*` when they are set. Do not
  change the git identity in the repository or in the global config.
- GitHub: git over HTTPS uses the `gh` credential helper, which the
  entrypoint configures from `GH_TOKEN`. Use `gh` for issues, pull requests
  and releases; it reads `GH_TOKEN` from the environment.
- GitLab (optional): when `GITLAB_TOKEN` is set, git over HTTPS to the
  GitLab host (`GITLAB_URL`, default `https://gitlab.com`) is preconfigured
  by the entrypoint. Use `glab` for issues, MRs, pipelines and releases (it
  reads `GITLAB_TOKEN`; pass `--hostname` for self-hosted instances) or the
  REST API with the `PRIVATE-TOKEN` header.
- Forgejo (optional): when `FORGEJO_TOKEN` and `FORGEJO_URL` are set, git
  over HTTPS/HTTP to that instance is preconfigured by the entrypoint. Use
  the REST API (`<FORGEJO_URL>/api/v1/...`) with the `Authorization: token`
  header.
- Never print, log or commit `GH_TOKEN`, `GITLAB_TOKEN`, `FORGEJO_TOKEN` or
  other credentials.

## Container updates

OpenCode is baked into the image; it cannot update itself inside the
container. Never run `opencode upgrade` or edit the installed binary. Updates
are published by the GitHub Actions workflow, so ask the user to pull a newer
image when a newer OpenCode is needed.

## Models

No model is pinned in the baked config. Until the user connects a provider,
OpenCode serves its free built-in models (provider `opencode`) with no
account or key, and the session starts on one of them.

When the session runs on a free built-in model, mention it once at the start
of the conversation (in the user's language, one or two sentences): the
session runs on a free model that ships with OpenCode, and for other models
the user can connect a provider with the TUI's `/connect` command and then
pick a model in the model picker. The TUI's sidebar already shows the
`/connect` hint, so keep the mention brief.

If the user asks about an environment file instead, offer to create a `.env`
file in the project folder yourself: copy the template
`/home/opencode/.env.example` to `.env` in the working directory (the project
is mounted, so the file lands on the host), and tell the user to fill in
`OPENROUTER_API_KEY` and add `--env-file .env` to the run command (the
optional launcher finds the file on its own).

Offer it once; do not repeat it unless the user asks, and do not push it if
the user is content with the built-in model.

## Secrets

Secrets (provider API keys, the server password, forge tokens) are passed at
runtime through the environment, or stored once by the user with
`opencode auth login` or the TUI's `/connect` command (a stored account wins
over the matching environment
variable, for example over `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`). The runtime env template is
baked into the image at `/home/opencode/.env.example`. When a required
variable is missing or empty, use the `env-setup` skill to offer the user a
copy of the template. Never write secrets into the repository, print them in
output, commit a `.env` file, or run `opencode auth export`.

## sudo

Passwordless sudo is available inside this container. Use it only to install
software that is missing for the current task.

Allowed:

- `sudo apk add --no-cache <package>` after checking the package name with
  `apk search <package>`.
- Temporary build dependencies via `--virtual`, removed in the same session.

Not allowed:

- Editing, creating, moving or deleting project files through sudo. Container
  root maps to a subuid on the host and would break project file ownership.
  All project changes go through the normal user.
- Running the agent, git, or language tooling as root.
- `apk upgrade`, `apk del` of base packages, or replacing system runtimes.
- Installing language packages with sudo: use project-local tooling, `mise`,
  `uv`, or `npm install`. A global CLI is the exception, not the default.
- Changing `/etc/sudoers*`, `/etc/passwd`, or SSH/GPG configuration.

Rules:

- State the package and the reason before installing, and keep it minimal.
- Runtime installs live in the writable layer and disappear when the
  container exits. If a tool is needed permanently, tell the user so it can be
  added to the Containerfile.
- After installing, verify with `command -v <tool>` and the tool's version.
- Never use sudo to work around a permission error inside the project; fix
  the cause or ask the user.

# Env setup

Use this skill when a required runtime environment variable is missing or
empty, or when a model or provider request fails with an authentication
error (for example HTTP 401, "missing API key", or a provider reporting no
credentials).

The image ships a documented runtime env template at
`/home/opencode/.env.example`. Values are passed at runtime only (`--env-file`
or a Kubernetes Secret) and are never baked into the image.

No key is required for the free built-in models: until the user connects a
provider, the session runs on OpenCode's free models (provider `opencode`).
The OpenRouter key is only needed for OpenRouter models; it arrives either in
the environment (`OPENROUTER_API_KEY`) or as a stored account from the TUI's
`/connect` command or `opencode auth login openrouter`. If the user wants
OpenRouter models and the key is missing or invalid, copying the template
does not fix it: tell the user to connect in the TUI with `/connect` (the key
is stored on the state volume) or to set `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` in
the env file and restart. Use this skill for the remaining variables.

## Check

List which variables are currently set:

```sh
env | grep -E '^(OPENROUTER_API_KEY|OPENCODE_PASSWORD|GH_TOKEN|GITLAB_TOKEN|FORGEJO_TOKEN)=' || true
```

## Actions

1. List the missing variables in a table with their purpose. The template at
   `/home/opencode/.env.example` documents every variable.
2. Offer to copy the template into the working folder (the project directory
   is mounted from the host, so the file ends up on the host):

   ```sh
   cp /home/opencode/.env.example .env
   ```

3. Explain that the user fills in the values on the host and restarts the
   container with the file:

   - Docker/Podman: add `--env-file .env` to the run command and start the
     container again.
   - Kubernetes: update the `Secret` referenced by the Deployment and let
     the pod restart.

4. Remind the user:

   - Add `.env` to `.gitignore`; never commit the file.
   - Keep it readable only by the user: `chmod 600 .env`.
   - Never print or echo the values, and never write them into the
     repository or the logs.

## Variables

| Variable                                     | Purpose                                                                                                                                  |
| -------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`                         | API key for OpenRouter models. Optional: the free built-in models work without it; the stored account wins over this variable.           |
| `OPENCODE_PASSWORD`                          | Password for the OpenCode server (HTTP API). Optional: when empty, the server generates one and prints it to the container log on start. |
| `GH_TOKEN`                                   | GitHub token for git over HTTPS and the `gh` CLI. Optional.                                                                              |
| `GITLAB_TOKEN`                               | GitLab token for git over HTTPS, the `glab` CLI and API calls. Optional.                                                                 |
| `GITLAB_URL`                                 | Self-hosted GitLab host (default `https://gitlab.com`). Optional.                                                                        |
| `FORGEJO_URL`                                | Forgejo/Gitea instance URL; required for `FORGEJO_TOKEN`. Optional.                                                                      |
| `FORGEJO_TOKEN`                              | Forgejo/Gitea token for git and the REST API. Optional.                                                                                  |
| `GIT_AUTHOR_NAME` / `GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL`       | Author identity for git commits. Optional.                                                                                               |
| `GIT_COMMITTER_NAME` / `GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL` | Committer identity for git commits. Optional.                                                                                            |

# opencode-typescript

[![Build](https://github.com/app/opencode-typescript/actions/workflows/build.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/app/opencode-typescript/actions/workflows/build.yml)
[![Last build](https://img.shields.io/endpoint?url=https%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fapp%2Fopencode-typescript%2Fstatus%2Fstatus.json)](https://github.com/app/opencode-typescript/actions/workflows/build.yml)

A container image that runs [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) for TypeScript
development. Nothing to install: one run command from your project directory
and the agent is working — the TUI opens inside the container.

## Quick start

From the project directory you want the agent to work in:

Podman:

```bash
podman run -it --rm --userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000 \
  -v "$PWD:/home/opencode/projects/$(basename "$PWD")" \
  -v opencode-state-$(id -un):/home/opencode/.local \
  --detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q" \
  ghcr.io/app/opencode-typescript:latest
```

Docker (the same, with `--user` instead of `--userns`):

```bash
docker run -it --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  -v "$PWD:/home/opencode/projects/$(basename "$PWD")" \
  -v opencode-state-$(id -un):/home/opencode/.local \
  --detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q" \
  ghcr.io/app/opencode-typescript:latest
```

State (sessions, connected accounts) is kept in the per-user volume
`opencode-state-<user>`, so users of a shared machine do not share it. The
TUI opens on OpenCode's free built-in model — start typing, no key needed.
For other models, connect OpenRouter with the TUI's `/connect` command and
pick a model in the model picker. See [Installation](docs/installation.md).

## The image

- **Rolling latest.** GitHub Actions builds and publishes the image to GHCR on
  every push and on a schedule, always with the current upstream OpenCode and
  Node LTS versions. Tags: `latest`,
  `oc-<opencode-version>-node<node-version>`, `<YYYYMMDD>` — see
  [Updating](docs/updating.md).
- **TypeScript toolchain.** Current Node LTS via mise, TypeScript and the
  TypeScript language server, Prettier, pnpm/yarn, git and the usual agent
  tooling — see [Toolchain](docs/toolchain.md).
- **Non-root.** The agent never runs as root: on Podman it is the image's
  uid 1000 mapped onto your host user, on Docker your host UID, with a
  restricted sudo policy.

## Three kinds of users

- A human in the TUI — the image default, as in the quick start above.
- A human in the web UI — server mode plus the pairing flow.
- An external agent — server mode plus the HTTP API (Basic auth, username
  `opencode`).

Server mode is an explicit command
(`opencode serve --hostname 0.0.0.0 --port 4096`); see
[Usage](docs/usage.md) and [Access](docs/api.md). Running OpenCode in
Kubernetes: [Kubernetes](docs/kubernetes.md).

## Security and secrets

OpenCode runs unprivileged (uid 1000 mapped onto your host user on Podman,
your host UID on Docker) with a restricted sudo policy, so treat the
container as the security boundary. Secrets live only on the host or on the
`opencode-state-<user>` volume: the runtime env file, the calling environment, a
Kubernetes Secret, or a connected account. Nothing secret is baked into the
image; it ships a documented `.env.example` template, and a built-in agent
skill offers to copy it into the working folder when runtime variables are
missing. See [Security notes](docs/security.md).

## Documentation

| Document                                   | Contents                                                          |
| ------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [Installation](docs/installation.md)       | Requirements, the first run, more models, the optional launcher   |
| [Usage](docs/usage.md)                     | Running the container, mounts, passing secrets, command overrides |
| [Access](docs/api.md)                      | TUI, web UI and the HTTP API for agents, Basic auth, OpenAPI      |
| [Kubernetes](docs/kubernetes.md)           | Deployment, Service and Secret examples for server mode           |
| [Toolchain](docs/toolchain.md)             | Installed tools, Node.js and mise, installing extra packages      |
| [Architecture](docs/architecture.md)       | Repository layout, the image, the GitHub Actions pipeline         |
| [Updating](docs/updating.md)               | How versions are resolved and how image releases work             |
| [Security notes](docs/security.md)         | Trust model and secret handling                                   |
| [Troubleshooting](docs/troubleshooting.md) | Common errors and fixes                                           |

# Access

How the three kinds of users reach the agent. OpenCode lives only inside the
container; nothing is installed on the host.

## TUI

The image default. From the project directory:

```bash
podman run -it --rm --userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000 \
  -v "$PWD:/home/opencode/projects/$(basename "$PWD")" \
  -v opencode-state-$(id -un):/home/opencode/.local \
  --detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q" \
  ghcr.io/app/opencode-typescript:latest
```

See [Usage](usage.md#open-the-tui-default) for the mount layout (Docker:
the same with `--user` instead of `--userns`). The TUI talks to the local
process inside
the container and needs no password.

## Web UI

The web UI is served by the [server mode](usage.md#start-the-server-web-ui-http-api).
To sign in, create a pairing link from inside the running container:

Podman:

```bash
podman exec -it --detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q" opencode opencode pair
```

Docker:

```bash
docker exec -it --detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q" opencode opencode pair
```

Open the printed link in a browser (the port must be published,
`-p 4096:4096`). Links work once and expire in 5 minutes; sessions last
30 days. Changing the server password signs every session out. Over SSH,
forward the server port and open the link locally.

## Authentication

Server mode is password-protected. Set `OPENCODE_PASSWORD` in the env file to
use a fixed password; when it is empty, the server generates a random one and
prints it to the container log on start. HTTP clients use Basic auth: the
username is always `opencode`, and only the password can be changed.

## HTTP API (agents)

Start the server explicitly (see
[Usage](usage.md#start-the-server-web-ui-http-api)), then an external agent
creates a session and sends prompts through the REST API:

```bash
BASE=http://localhost:4096
AUTH="opencode:a-long-secret"

# Server info (also a good health check)
curl -fsS -u "$AUTH" "$BASE/api/info"

# Create a session
SESSION=$(curl -fsS -u "$AUTH" -X POST "$BASE/api/session" | jq -r .id)

# Send a prompt
curl -fsS -u "$AUTH" -X POST "$BASE/api/session/$SESSION/prompt" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"parts": [{"type": "text", "text": "Summarize this repository"}]}'

# Subscribe to server events
curl -fsS -u "$AUTH" -N "$BASE/api/event"
```

- The OpenAPI 3.1 document of a running server is served at
  `http://localhost:4096/openapi.json`; the published reference lives at
  <https://opencode.ai/docs/openapi.json>.
- The generated TypeScript client is `@opencode/client` (Promise-based
  resource clients and async iterables for streaming endpoints).
- Permission requests: the baked configuration allows `edit`, `shell` and
  `webfetch` autonomously; for `ask` outcomes, clients reply through
  `POST /api/session/{sessionID}/permission/{requestID}/reply`
  (`once`, `always`, `reject`).
- See <https://opencode.ai/docs/api> for the full endpoint reference.

## Pairing from the server side

`POST /api/pair` creates a pairing code and `GET /auth/connect/{code}`
redeems it; the `opencode pair` command wraps this flow.

# Architecture

Repository layout, the image, and the GitHub Actions pipeline.

## Layout

```text
.
├── AGENTS.md                         # instructions for agents working on this repository
├── bin/opencode-ts                   # launcher: thin wrapper over podman/docker
├── Containerfile                     # OpenCode image + toolchain, built-in non-root user (uid 1000)
├── .env.example                      # runtime env template (copied into the image)
├── versions.json                     # pinned toolchain versions (updated by the bot PR)
├── .github/workflows/build.yml       # build, publish, smoke test, pin updates
├── scripts/
│   └── resolve-versions.sh           # resolves the current OpenCode and Node LTS
├── config/
│   ├── bin/entrypoint.sh             # git identity, forge credentials, cd into the project, exec "$@"
│   ├── gitconfig                     # generic gitconfig for the non-root user
│   ├── mise/config.toml              # mise settings (musl, slow-mirror timeouts)
│   ├── sudoers.d/opencode            # passwordless sudo policy (any user in the container)
│   └── opencode/                     # copied to /home/opencode/.config/opencode
│       ├── opencode.jsonc            # permissions, LSP (no model or provider pinned)
│       ├── AGENTS.md                 # agent instructions (public, no personal data)
│       └── skills/env-setup/SKILL.md # offers the env template when runtime variables are missing
├── k8s/
│   ├── deployment.yaml
│   ├── service.yaml
│   └── secret.example.yaml
├── docs/                             # detailed documentation
└── README.md
```

## Image

`Containerfile` extends `ghcr.io/anomalyco/opencode:<version>` with the
[toolchain](toolchain.md) and a non-root `opencode` user (uid/gid 1000 by
default, overridable with `--build-arg UID=... --build-arg GID=...`). The
documented run commands make the image's user the caller's: Podman maps it
onto the host user with `--userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000`, Docker
overrides it with `--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"`, so files created by the agent
keep host ownership either way. The home and mise directories are
world-writable inside the image so that any user the container runs as can
write to them (the container is a single-user trust boundary). The upstream
version and the Node LTS version are build args supplied by the workflow;
they are never hardcoded and are recorded as image labels
(`org.opencode-typescript.opencode`, `org.opencode-typescript.node`).

The image bakes configuration, not secrets:

- `config/opencode/` → `/home/opencode/.config/opencode/` (autonomous
  permissions, the TypeScript LSP, the `env-setup` skill, the `AGENTS.md`
  policy; no model or provider is pinned — the session runs on OpenCode's
  free built-in models until the user connects OpenRouter);
- `config/gitconfig` → `/home/opencode/.gitconfig` (generic identity);
- `.env.example` → `/home/opencode/.env.example` (the runtime env template);
- `config/bin/entrypoint.sh` → `/usr/local/bin/entrypoint.sh` (git identity
  from the environment, forge git credentials from `GH_TOKEN`,
  `GITLAB_TOKEN`, `FORGEJO_TOKEN` when set, a `cd` into the single mounted
  project when there is one, then `exec "$@"`).

The default command is the interactive TUI: `docker run -it ... image` opens
a session with no OpenCode installation on the host, in the mounted project
(the entrypoint `cd`s into it when it is the only project mount). The server
(`opencode serve --hostname 0.0.0.0 --port 4096`) is started explicitly —
the k8s deployment and the CI smoke test pass it as the container command.
See [Usage](usage.md) and [Access](api.md).

## CI pipeline

`.github/workflows/build.yml` runs on push to `main`, on a daily schedule, and
on demand (`workflow_dispatch`):

1. `scripts/resolve-versions.sh` resolves the latest stable OpenCode tag from
   the upstream GHCR image and the current Node LTS from
   `nodejs.org/dist/index.json`.
2. Buildx builds `linux/amd64` and pushes to GHCR with the tags `latest`,
   `oc-<opencode>-node<node>` and `<YYYYMMDD>`. The layer cache lives in a
   separate `opencode-typescript-buildcache` GHCR repository.
3. A smoke test asserts that the image default stays the TUI, starts the
   server explicitly, waits for `GET /api/info` with Basic auth, and checks
   the reported version.
4. The `update-pins` job re-resolves the versions and, when they differ from
   `versions.json` in the repository, opens a pull request updating the pins
   (`peter-evans/create-pull-request`). Merging it rebuilds and republishes
   the image. See [Updating](updating.md).

# Installation

How to open the first session. There is nothing to install: the image is
pulled automatically on the first run, and the TUI runs inside the container,
so no OpenCode client is needed on the host.

## Requirements

- [Docker](https://www.docker.com/) or [rootless Podman](https://podman.io/).
  For Podman, enable subuid mappings so the
  `--userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000` flag works (`subuid`/`subgid` entries
  in `/etc/subuid` and `/etc/subgid`).
- Nothing else: OpenCode's free built-in models work without any account or
  key. An [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/) API key is optional — see
  [More models](#more-models-optional).

## Open the first session

From the project directory you want the agent to work in:

Podman:

```bash
podman run -it --rm --userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000 \
  -v "$PWD:/home/opencode/projects/$(basename "$PWD")" \
  -v opencode-state-$(id -un):/home/opencode/.local \
  --detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q" \
  ghcr.io/app/opencode-typescript:latest
```

Docker (the same, with `--user` instead of `--userns`):

```bash
docker run -it --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  -v "$PWD:/home/opencode/projects/$(basename "$PWD")" \
  -v opencode-state-$(id -un):/home/opencode/.local \
  --detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q" \
  ghcr.io/app/opencode-typescript:latest
```

`--userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000` (Podman) maps the image's built-in user
(uid 1000) onto your host user, so files the agent creates are uid 1000 in
the container and yours on the host; the Docker command passes `--user
"$(id -u):$(id -g)"` instead, running the agent as your host UID directly.

The TUI opens inside the container; the project is mounted read-write at
`/home/opencode/projects/<name>` and OpenCode starts inside it, so the
session opens your project directly. The `opencode-state-<user>` volume
(one per user) keeps credentials and the session database across runs. The session starts on OpenCode's free built-in model — start typing
right away, no key needed; the sidebar's `/connect` hint leads to other
models (see [More models](#more-models-optional)).

## More models (optional)

The free built-in models need no key. To use OpenRouter models, connect
OpenRouter once; two ways, and when both are present, the stored account
wins.

### Option 1: connect in the TUI (`/connect`)

With the TUI open, type `/connect`, pick OpenRouter, and enter the API key.
The credential is stored in your `opencode-state-<user>` volume, so every later run
has the models. The same credential can be stored from the host without the
TUI:

```bash
podman run -it --rm --userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000 \
  -v opencode-state-$(id -un):/home/opencode/.local \
  --detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q" \
  ghcr.io/app/opencode-typescript:latest opencode auth login openrouter
```

The same works with Docker (with `--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"` instead of
`--userns`). Remove the stored key the same way, with `opencode auth logout
openrouter` in place of `auth login openrouter`.

### Option 2: environment file

Keep the key on the host: put it in a `.env` file in the project folder —
ask the agent to create it (it copies the template from the image into the
current folder, which is on the host), or copy
[.env.example](../.env.example) from the repository — fill in
`OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, keep it private with `chmod 600 .env` and add it to
`.gitignore`, and pass it on the run command:

```bash
podman run -it --rm --userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000 \
  -v "$PWD:/home/opencode/projects/$(basename "$PWD")" \
  -v opencode-state-$(id -un):/home/opencode/.local \
  --detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q" \
  --env-file .env \
  ghcr.io/app/opencode-typescript:latest
```

The same works with Docker (with `--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"` instead of
`--userns`). See [Security notes](security.md) for how secrets are handled.

Either way, the OpenRouter models then appear in the TUI's model picker —
pick the one you want to work with; the pick is remembered on the
`opencode-state-<user>` volume and used on later runs.

## The launcher (optional)

The repository ships `bin/opencode-ts`, a thin wrapper over podman/docker for
people who prefer a shorter command: it resolves the engine (Podman first,
override with `OPENCODE_TS_ENGINE`), mounts the current project and the
`opencode-state-<user>` volume, finds the env file on its own
(`OPENCODE_TS_ENV_FILE` → `./.env` → `~/.config/opencode-typescript/env`), and
passes all remaining arguments to opencode unchanged. Fetch the single file
from the repository and install it:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/app/opencode-typescript/main/bin/opencode-ts \
  -o /tmp/opencode-ts
install -m755 /tmp/opencode-ts "$HOME/.local/bin/opencode-ts"
```

Then run `opencode-ts` from the project directory (`opencode-ts -r
../frontend` mounts a sibling read-only, `OPENCODE_TS_RUN_ARGS="-p 4096:4096"`
publishes the port in server mode). It is optional: every launcher flag has a
plain `run` equivalent shown in [Usage](usage.md).

## Image tags

The image is published to GHCR by the GitHub Actions workflow. Tags:
`latest`, `oc-<opencode-version>-node<node-version>` (the exact toolchain
combination) and `<YYYYMMDD>` (build date). See [Updating](updating.md) for
how versions are chosen.

## Uninstall

Remove the image and the state volume:

```bash
podman rmi ghcr.io/app/opencode-typescript:latest
podman volume rm opencode-state-$(id -un)
```

# Kubernetes

Running the OpenCode server in a cluster with the example manifests in
`k8s/`.

## Prerequisites

- A Kubernetes cluster and `kubectl`.
- A pull secret for GHCR (replace the placeholders):

  ```bash
  kubectl create secret docker-registry ghcr-pull \
    --docker-server=https://ghcr.io \
    --docker-username=<you> \
    --docker-password=<ghcr-token>
  ```

- A runtime `Secret` based on [k8s/secret.example.yaml](../k8s/secret.example.yaml)
  with real values, applied to the target namespace.

## Deploy

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
kubectl apply -f k8s/service.yaml
```

The deployment pins the image's built-in user (uid/gid 1000): the image
default is the interactive TUI, so the manifest passes the server command
explicitly in the container `args`. It keeps credentials and the session database on the
`opencode-state` PVC and mounts an `emptyDir` as the agent working space. It
uses `Recreate` because a single writer owns the state volume.

The Service exposes port 4096 as `ClusterIP` by default; switch `type` to
`LoadBalancer` for external access.

## Access

```bash
kubectl port-forward svc/opencode 4096:4096
```

Then use the HTTP API as described in [Access](api.md#http-api-agents) with
`http://localhost:4096` and your `OPENCODE_PASSWORD`.

## Notes

- Probes are TCP, because the HTTP API requires Basic auth and probes cannot
  send credentials.
- The `emptyDir` project volume is wiped when the pod restarts. Replace it
  with a `PersistentVolumeClaim` or a projected volume when the project must
  persist.
- Update the `image` field (or pin the `oc-<version>-node<version>` tag
  instead of `latest`) when you move to a new release; see
  [Updating](updating.md).
- Secrets in the `Secret` are visible to the pod; treat the pod as trusted
  for them, as documented in [Security notes](security.md).

# Security notes

## Trust model

- OpenCode never runs as root: in every documented mode it is the image's
  built-in user, uid/gid 1000 (Podman maps it onto your host user with
  `--userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000`; Docker runs it as your host UID with
  `--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"`; the k8s manifest pins `runAsUser: 1000`).
  That user has passwordless sudo; the policy is broad by design
  (`NOPASSWD: ALL`) and constrained by the usage rules in the baked
  `AGENTS.md`. The home and mise directories are world-writable inside the
  image so any `--user` can write to them. Container root maps to a subuid
  on the host (rootless Podman) or to root in the pod (Kubernetes). Treat
  the container as the security boundary: the agent can effectively do
  anything the container can.
- The baked permissions allow the agent to `edit` files, run `shell`
  commands, and `webfetch` URLs without prompts, so it works autonomously.
  Only mount projects and tokens the agent is allowed to touch.
- The container runs the agent, not your desktop: do not mount sensitive
  host directories (SSH agent, cloud credentials) unless the task needs them.

## Secrets

- Secrets live only on the host or on the state volume: the runtime env file
  (`chmod 600`), the calling environment, a Kubernetes `Secret`, or a
  connected account (`opencode auth login`). Nothing secret is baked into the
  image; the image ships the documented template
  (`/home/opencode/.env.example`) instead.
- Every process in the container, including the agent, sees the forwarded
  variables. A forge token (`GH_TOKEN`, `GITLAB_TOKEN`, `FORGEJO_TOKEN`) is
  usable by the agent for anything that token can do — prefer a dedicated
  token with the minimum scopes.
- The `OPENCODE_PASSWORD` (or the generated one printed to the log) protects
  the HTTP API with Basic auth in server mode. Keep the log private when the
  password is generated.
- The state volume (`/home/opencode/.local`) holds provider credentials and
  the session database; treat it as sensitive.
- Never commit a `.env` file. The `env-setup` skill keeps the agent from
  writing secrets into the repository and reminds about `chmod 600`.

## Network

- In server mode the server listens on `0.0.0.0` inside the container. Expose
  the port only to the networks that need it (host port, `ClusterIP` service,
  or a `LoadBalancer` with authentication in front). The default TUI mode does
  not listen on any port.
- Pairing links are single-use and expire in 5 minutes; web sessions last
  30 days and are revoked when the password changes.

# Toolchain

The image is built for TypeScript agent work: search, Node.js, TypeScript
tooling and native build tools are available out of the box.

| Area       | Tools                                                                                                      |
| ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Search     | `rg` (ripgrep), `fd`, `ast-grep` (`sg`)                                                                    |
| Data       | `jq`, `yq`                                                                                                 |
| Node.js    | `mise`, current Node LTS, `npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn`                                                            |
| TypeScript | `typescript` (`tsc`), `typescript-language-server`, `prettier`                                             |
| Python     | `python3`, `uv`                                                                                            |
| Git        | `git`, `openssh-client`, `gh`, `glab`                                                                      |
| Build      | `gcc`/`g++`, `make`, `linux-headers`, `pkgconf`, `openssl-dev` (node-gyp)                                  |
| Shell      | `bash`, `shellcheck`, `shfmt`, GNU userland (`coreutils`, `findutils`, `grep`, `sed`, `gawk`, `diffutils`) |
| Misc       | `less`, `file`, `tree`, `curl`, `xz`, `unzip`, `zip`, `tzdata`                                             |

System tools are the GNU versions, not BusyBox applets, so commands that rely
on GNU flags work as expected.

## Node.js

Node is managed by [mise](https://mise.jdx.dev). The Node LTS current at
build time is installed at image build time (recorded in `versions.json` and
in the image labels) and is the default:

```bash
node -v                      # the Node LTS pinned at build time
mise ls                      # installed and active versions
mise x node@22 -- npm ci     # run a command with another version
```

`.nvmrc`, `.node-version`, `.tool-versions` and `mise.toml` in the mounted
project are honored automatically. A version that is not installed yet is
downloaded on demand; on x86_64 the pinned version comes from the official
musl builds at nodejs.org, and other versions and architectures use
`unofficial-builds.nodejs.org` (slow). `pnpm` and `yarn` go through Corepack
(installed from npm, since Node 25 no longer ships it) and follow
`packageManager` in `package.json`.

## TypeScript

`typescript`, `typescript-language-server` and `prettier` are installed
globally for the pinned Node at build time. The language server is wired into
OpenCode through the baked configuration (`lsp.typescript`), covering
`.ts`, `.tsx`, `.js`, `.jsx`, `.mjs`, `.cjs`, `.mts`, `.cts`.

## Python

`python3` comes from Alpine and `uv` manages virtual environments and
packages:

```bash
uv venv
uv pip install -r requirements.txt
uvx ruff check .
```

Do not install packages into the system interpreter with `pip`.

## Installing extra packages

The user the container runs as has passwordless sudo (the policy matches
any user), so the agent can install Alpine packages when a task needs them:

```bash
sudo apk add --no-cache <package>
```

Runtime installs are not persisted: they disappear with the container. Add
the package to the `Containerfile` for a permanent tool. The usage policy is
defined in the baked `AGENTS.md`; see [Security notes](security.md).

# Troubleshooting

Common errors and fixes.

## The TUI does not start or looks broken

- The TUI needs an interactive terminal: run the container with `-it`.
  Without a TTY the TUI cannot start.
- No colors or a garbled screen: `TERM` is inherited from the calling
  environment, so make sure it is set on the host (for example
  `xterm-256color`).
- The TUI talks to the local process inside the container and needs no
  password; if a provider error appears, check the OpenRouter key (below).
- The default command is the TUI; if the container starts a server instead,
  either a custom command was passed (for example by the k8s manifest) or the
  local image is stale. `podman run` and `docker run` reuse a local image
  without re-pulling it: run
  `podman pull ghcr.io/app/opencode-typescript:latest` and start again.
- The TUI opens at `/home/opencode/projects` instead of your project: that
  is expected when several projects are mounted (or none). Open a specific
  project by appending its directory to the run command:
  `opencode /home/opencode/projects/<name>`.
- `ctrl-p` (the command palette) does nothing: your run command lacks
  `--detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q"`. The default detach sequence of
  podman/docker is `ctrl-p ctrl-q`, so the engine waits for `ctrl-q` and
  the key never reaches the TUI. Every command in this repository carries
  the flag; alternatively set `detachKeys` in your engine's client config
  file.

## The server does not respond (server mode)

- Server mode is an explicit command: the container must be started with
  `opencode serve --hostname 0.0.0.0 --port 4096` (the k8s manifest and the
  CI smoke test do this; the image default is the TUI).
- Check the container is running and the port is published:
  `podman ps` / `docker ps`, and the `-p 4096:4096` flag.
- The server binds `0.0.0.0:4096` inside the container; without the port
  publication the host cannot reach it.
- Give it a few seconds on first start, then check the log for the
  `server listening on http://0.0.0.0:4096` line: `podman logs opencode`.
- In Kubernetes, the pod must be `Ready` (TCP probe) and the Service must
  select `app: opencode`; `kubectl port-forward svc/opencode 4096:4096`.

## Authentication errors (HTTP 401, server mode)

- The username is always `opencode`; only the password changes.
- When `OPENCODE_PASSWORD` is empty, the server generated a password and
  printed it to the container log on start (`podman logs opencode`,
  `kubectl logs deploy/opencode`).
- Pairing links for the web UI do not use the password at all; the browser
  session is created through the one-time link.

## No model or provider errors

- A 401/"missing API key" from OpenRouter means the container has no OpenRouter
  key: neither `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` in the environment nor a connected
  account. Connect once in the TUI with `/connect` (the key is stored on
  your `opencode-state-<user>` volume), or set the variable in the env file
  (or the
  Kubernetes Secret) and restart with `--env-file` / the updated Secret.
- Without any key the TUI opens on a free built-in model and the agent
  answers without a key. For more models, connect OpenRouter (see
  [Installation](installation.md#more-models-optional)).
- When the agent is running and another variable (for example a forge token)
  is missing, the `env-setup` skill offers to copy the template from
  `/home/opencode/.env.example` into the working folder.

## Git operations fail

- Git over HTTPS is preconfigured by the entrypoint from the tokens in the
  container environment: `GH_TOKEN` (GitHub, via `gh auth setup-git`),
  `GITLAB_TOKEN` (+ `GITLAB_URL`) and `FORGEJO_TOKEN` (+ `FORGEJO_URL`).
  Check that the token for the host you push to is set.
- Commits are signed with the `GIT_AUTHOR_*` / `GIT_COMMITTER_*` variables or
  the baked generic identity; set the variables in the env file.
- Permission denied on files in the project (the agent cannot create, edit
  or commit): the run command must carry the user mapping —
  `--userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000` (Podman) or `--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"`
  (Docker), so files it writes are owned by your host user (every command in
  [Usage](usage.md) includes it). A state volume created by an older image
  needs a one-time removal first (Usage, Mounts).

## Node version problems in the project

- A version requested by `.nvmrc`/`mise.toml` that is not installed is
  downloaded on demand; on non-x86_64 or for older versions this uses the
  slow `unofficial-builds.nodejs.org` mirror (mise is configured with long
  timeouts and retries for that).
- `mise ls` shows installed versions; the pinned LTS is recorded in the image
  labels (`docker image inspect`).

## The image looks stale

- Pull the tag you expect: `docker pull ghcr.io/app/opencode-typescript:latest`
  and compare the labels with the current pins in `versions.json`.
- To force a new build without waiting for the schedule, run the
  `Build` workflow from the repository's Actions page.

# Updating

How versions are chosen and how image releases work.

## Rolling latest

The image always builds with the current upstream versions — there is nothing
to update on the host:

- **OpenCode**: `scripts/resolve-versions.sh` pages through the tag list of
  `ghcr.io/anomalyco/opencode` (anonymous GHCR token, `Link` header
  pagination) and keeps the newest semver tag, ignoring prereleases and
  moving tags.
- **Node LTS**: the newest entry with a truthy `lts` in
  `https://nodejs.org/dist/index.json`.
- **npm globals** (`typescript`, `typescript-language-server`, `prettier`):
  whatever is published on build day.

The workflow resolves them on every run (push to `main`, the daily schedule,
or `workflow_dispatch`) and rebuilds the image.

## Image tags

| Tag                                        | Meaning                                      |
| ------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------- |
| `latest`                                   | the newest published build                   |
| `oc-<opencode-version>-node<node-version>` | the exact toolchain combination, for pinning |
| `<YYYYMMDD>`                               | the build date                               |

Run the version that was current when you read the docs, or pin:

```bash
docker pull ghcr.io/app/opencode-typescript:oc-2.3.0-node26.13.1
```

`docker image inspect` prints the pinned versions from the image labels.

## Pin updates in the repository

`versions.json` records the last resolved toolchain combination. The
`update-pins` job opens a pull request (branch
`chore/update-pinned-versions`) whenever the resolved versions differ from
the file. Merging the PR rebuilds and republishes the image; the schedule
keeps looking for newer versions on its own.

## Building locally

For a one-off build with a specific upstream version:

```bash
docker build \
  --build-arg OPENCODE_VERSION=2.3.0 \
  --build-arg NODE_VERSION=26.13.1 \
  -t opencode-typescript:local .
```

The `Containerfile` never hardcodes versions, so the workflow remains the
source of truth.

# Usage

Running the container: the TUI, the server mode, mounts, and secrets.

## Open the TUI (default)

The default command is the interactive TUI inside the container. From the
project directory:

Podman:

```bash
podman run -it --rm --userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000 \
  -v "$PWD:/home/opencode/projects/$(basename "$PWD")" \
  -v opencode-state-$(id -un):/home/opencode/.local \
  --detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q" \
  ghcr.io/app/opencode-typescript:latest
```

Docker (the same, with `--user` instead of `--userns`):

```bash
docker run -it --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  -v "$PWD:/home/opencode/projects/$(basename "$PWD")" \
  -v opencode-state-$(id -un):/home/opencode/.local \
  --detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q" \
  ghcr.io/app/opencode-typescript:latest
```

No server, no published port, and nothing installed on the host. The project
directory is mounted read-write at `/home/opencode/projects/<name>`; when it
is the only project mount, OpenCode starts inside it, so the TUI opens your
project directly. If you have a `.env` file (see
[More models](installation.md#more-models-optional)), add `--env-file .env`
to the command. The optional [launcher](installation.md#the-launcher-optional)
wraps exactly this.

## Start the server (web UI, HTTP API)

Server mode is an explicit command on top of the same image:

```bash
podman run -d --name opencode --userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000 -p 4096:4096 \
  -v "$PWD:/home/opencode/projects/$(basename "$PWD")" \
  -v opencode-state-$(id -un):/home/opencode/.local \
  --env-file .env \
  ghcr.io/app/opencode-typescript:latest \
  opencode serve --hostname 0.0.0.0 --port 4096
```

The same works with Docker (with `--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"` instead of
`--userns`); drop `-d` and add `-it` for a foreground run. The [launcher](installation.md#the-launcher-optional)
equivalent is `OPENCODE_TS_RUN_ARGS="-p 4096:4096" opencode-ts serve
--hostname 0.0.0.0 --port 4096`.

To open the [web UI](api.md#web-ui), create a pairing link from inside the
running container:

Podman:

```bash
podman exec -it --detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q" opencode opencode pair
```

Docker:

```bash
docker exec -it --detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q" opencode opencode pair
```

and open the printed link in a browser. The [HTTP API](api.md#http-api-agents)
is available under Basic auth on the same port.

## Mounts

| Host path                      | Container path                   | Purpose                                                                          |
| ------------------------------ | -------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| your project directory         | `/home/opencode/projects/<name>` | the agent's working project; OpenCode starts inside it when it is the only mount |
| `opencode-state-<user>` volume | `/home/opencode/.local`          | credentials and the session database, one per user                               |

- User mapping: `--userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000` (Podman) runs the agent
  as the image's built-in user, uid/gid 1000, mapped onto your host user, so
  files it creates — in the project and on the state volume — are uid 1000 in
  the container and yours on the host. Docker has no user mapping, so its
  commands pass `--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"` instead, which runs the agent as
  your host UID with the same ownership outcome.
- `--detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q"` (in every command above) moves the
  engine's detach sequence off the default `ctrl-p ctrl-q`, which would
  swallow the TUI's `ctrl-p` command palette key.
- If you used an earlier version of this image, its state lived in a single
  shared volume, `opencode-state` (with permissions only uid 1000 could
  write). The commands above now use one volume per user,
  `opencode-state-<user>`; the old volume is simply not used anymore.
  Remove it when you no longer need it (`podman volume rm opencode-state`,
  or the Docker equivalent). Stored credentials are re-added with `/connect`.
- Mount sibling projects read-only with extra `-v` mounts under
  `/home/opencode/projects/`, for example
  `-v ../frontend:/home/opencode/projects/frontend:ro` (the launcher's
  `-r` flag wraps this). With several project mounts, OpenCode starts at
  the projects root; open a specific one by appending its directory to the
  run command: `opencode /home/opencode/projects/frontend`.
- For Kubernetes, see [Kubernetes](kubernetes.md) instead.

## Passing secrets

Secrets are never baked into the image; they are passed at runtime:

```bash
--env-file path/to/env            # one NAME=value per line
-e OPENROUTER_API_KEY=...         # or individual variables
```

The OpenRouter key is optional (the free built-in models need no key); to
connect, use the TUI's `/connect` command (see
[Installation](installation.md#more-models-optional)) — the stored account
wins over the environment.

By convention the file lives in the project directory (`.env`); the optional
[launcher](installation.md#the-launcher-optional) finds it on its own. The
template documenting every variable lives in the repository root
(`.env.example`) and inside the image at `/home/opencode/.env.example`.
Variable reference:

| Variable                                     | Required         | Purpose                                                              |
| -------------------------------------------- | ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`                         | no               | API key for OpenRouter models; the free built-in models need no key  |
| `OPENCODE_PASSWORD`                          | no (server mode) | server password; when empty, one is generated and printed to the log |
| `GH_TOKEN`                                   | no               | GitHub token for git over HTTPS and the `gh` CLI                     |
| `GITLAB_TOKEN`                               | no               | GitLab token for git, the `glab` CLI and the API                     |
| `GITLAB_URL`                                 | no               | self-hosted GitLab host (default `https://gitlab.com`)               |
| `FORGEJO_URL`                                | no               | Forgejo/Gitea instance URL, required for `FORGEJO_TOKEN`             |
| `FORGEJO_TOKEN`                              | no               | Forgejo token for git and the REST API                               |
| `GIT_AUTHOR_NAME` / `GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL`       | no               | author identity for commits                                          |
| `GIT_COMMITTER_NAME` / `GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL` | no               | committer identity for commits                                       |

When the agent is already running and a token or another variable is missing,
it can offer to copy the template into the working folder (the `env-setup`
skill). Never commit or print secrets; see [Security notes](security.md).

## Other commands

The entrypoint execs the command you pass, so any other opencode command or a
shell works — append it to the run command:

```bash
podman run -it --rm --userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000 \
  -v "$PWD:/home/opencode/projects/$(basename "$PWD")" \
  --detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q" \
  ghcr.io/app/opencode-typescript:latest \
  opencode run "Explain this repository"
```

That is a one-shot prompt with no server. For a shell inside the container,
replace the command with `bash`.

## Logs

Podman:

```bash
podman logs -f opencode
```

Docker:

```bash
docker logs -f opencode
```

In server mode, the generated server password (when `OPENCODE_PASSWORD` is
empty) is printed here on start.
